introduction: On this last Sunday of the Church's year we celebrate Jesus Christ, King of the Universe. His kingship is unlike any other. Ezekiel describes God as a shepherd who searches for the lost and binds up the wounded, and in the Gospel the King of glory identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner. Today is also World Youth Day in our dioceses. As we gather, let us welcome Christ as King of our hearts, our families and our world.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Christ our King came not to be served but to serve. With trust in his care, let us pray for all his people.
intentions: For the Church: that she may make the kingdom of Christ visible in the world, through truth spoken with love, through holiness of life, and through works of justice and peace. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the young people of our parish and of the world, on this World Youth Day: that they may know Christ as their friend and King and generously follow him. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the hungry, the sick, strangers and prisoners: that in them we may recognise and serve Christ himself. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are lost, scattered or wounded in body or spirit: that the Good Shepherd may seek them out and heal them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who have died: that Christ, the first fruits of those who have fallen asleep, may raise them to share his kingdom. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Almighty Father, you have given all things to your Son, the King of the universe. Hear our prayers, and make us faithful servants of his kingdom, now and at the end of time. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The King in disguise
reflection.body:
Kings in the ancient world often called themselves shepherds of their people. Ezekiel had watched Israel's rulers fail at that task, feeding themselves while the flock was scattered. So God makes a promise: "I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep." He will seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured and strengthen the weak. Today's feast tells us that the promise has been kept in Jesus.

The Gospel shows this Shepherd-King at the end of history. All nations are gathered before him, and he separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. The surprise is the question he asks. It is not about wealth or learning, not even about how often we spoke of religion. It is about bread, water, clothing, welcome, and visits to the sick and the imprisoned.

Even more surprising: both groups are astonished. "Lord, when did we see you?" The righteous did not know they were serving Christ; those who neglected the poor did not know they were neglecting him. The King has been in disguise all along, hidden in the least of his brothers and sisters. St Teresa of Calcutta used to count five words on the fingers of one hand, "you did it to me," so that she would never forget.

This is a sobering Gospel, and the Church does not soften its ending. Our choices matter eternally. But it is also deeply hopeful. Paul tells us that Christ has been raised as the first fruits; he must reign until every enemy is defeated, and the last enemy is death. The Kingdom is not a dream. It is already growing wherever someone feeds the hungry or visits the lonely in Christ's name.

We do not need to look far for our King. He is in the patient at the hospital, the migrant worker, the neighbour who is struggling, the young person looking for meaning. As this year closes and Advent approaches, let us ask him to reign in our hearts, and to open our eyes to see him where he hides.
